17. **How cities become free.** The ways a city breaks free of its master ("How cities become free"): conquered land not yet absorbed that revolts and breaks free ("Revolt follows conditions, not dice"); a governor who turns with the levies he raised, or a commander who keeps his army, and rules a city of his own, the new Idrimi; and a revolt with no one at its head raising a ruler from its own people ("A head rises where men lack one"). Each new free city is a power with a seat of its own, by the rules of item 11+. Built after item 13, since it needs governors and commanders, and after 11b's risen heads. Split from the city-states item on 21 October 2026, when city-states as powers moved forward to item 11+; a vassal who stops paying is free in practice already there. With revolt comes the gate opened from within, when a besieged city's hunger breaks its loyalty ("How long a siege lasts"). And an army living off the land angers its people (Haakon, 29 October 2026: "An army eating from the actual citizens stores then should make them pretty unhappy?", and to the design session's takes, "Yes, to all, expertly!"): troops taking food raise unrest by how much they take, their own king's included; every province carries unrest, the homeland too, though absorbed land starts loyal and needs far more to rise; each army buys its food where it stands by leave or takes it, as its king's order says once it arrives, but by need when it has no gold to buy with, and by its commander's choice once it has one, who may keep the gold sent for food and take anyway (Haakon, 29 October 2026: "But remember, when you say a king decides how his army supplies himself. Information time travel stoll applies. He can tell them to buy, but if he hasn't sent them enough money to buy with, they will do what they must to eat. And an army with an assigned commander (a character) the commander has the final say on following orders or not. He may keep any money meant for food, and just take instead."); and a ruler whose land was taken from remembers it as a grievance ("Revolt follows conditions, not dice" under War, "Armies need food as well as pay" under Land, people and economy). The script kings weigh buying against taking, and the item's report shows how often each is chosen and how often a homeland province rose. Whether a grant pays is the king's own sum, with no rule of its own (War, "Governors"; Haakon, 31 October 2026: "Yes, to all, expertly!"): its price, tribute and terms are whatever the two sides agree, and a script king grants only where tribute and price net him more than keeping the province would, after the frictions of distance and the risk of losing it. Scripts that grant are played against scripts that never do, on the same seeds; if granting never wins, the report says whether the scripts play it badly or the land's multiple makes land too dear to give away, a finding for item 18. Whom a province obeys (War, "Whom a province obeys"; Haakon, 31 October 2026: "Yes, please, expertly!"): no province is owned by a flag; each season it obeys whoever it fears or loves most, force (troops in or near it, against its own men) plus love (the ledger), and no one if nobody's weight clears what its people accept; conquest, revolt, absorption, turning and succession are this one rule; obedience has degrees by margin; the ledger starts as 1346 stood, with its divided loyalties seeded from the sources (Haakon, 31 October 2026: "Also, some of these seems to have "bands" of their own? Yes, expertly so!"); changes of hands need a clear margin and come as news with their cause; persons (kings, governors, vassals, every character) do not obey a ledger but choose by their stakes and the strategy their traits give them. Script kings use the census and judge their demands by their counts where it pays, measured against scripts that never count. **Stop for review.** Then **17+++, the season plays out** (31 October 2026; Haakon: "the player needs to feel the weight of the whole world, or it becomes meaningless to him/her.", then "Agreed, 100% sir!"): each season plays out on the map instead of jumping to the next picture. The season is the land's own state beneath the realms: snow, flood, green and drought are drawn on the ground under the realm colours, which lie over it as a light wash with clear borders so that nothing bleeds through, and the change moves (snow creeping down from the passes, the Nile rising along its banks, green spreading with the rains, the land browning from its edges); the season and drought textures are redrawn, painterly and quiet, after the period's own art, on the papyrus. Orders resolve in sequence: units travel their roads at their real pace, each drawn as what it is after the period's relics, a column as long as its men are many, dust behind marching troops, ships heeling under sail through the waves, an envoy's small caravan, and nothing teleports; battles flare as a clash with their outcome, sieges tighten, and the world acts on them visibly: storms at sea, snow in the passes, rivers in flood, an avalanche taking a column ("Winter is dangerous, never closed"). Pace by meaning, never faster than can be read: at fast speed the routine compresses while the great moments (a battle, a city falling, a disaster, an envoy's arrival) still play long enough to take in, and each season closes with a short line of what changed; top speed skips to the result only when chosen. The next season is computed while this one plays, so nobody waits and the frame never stutters. Only what the seat knows plays: a rival's army appears where it was seen, when the report arrives, and a disaster far away is news, not a scene; spectators and god view see everything move. Zoom shapes it too (Haakon: "If you are zoomed in near a unit in the waves, I want to hear it. And if I zoom in on the map, I like how Imperator makes the state color more and more transparent and you see the ground and effects under more clearly."): zoomed out, the realms' colours are full and the sound is the world's bed and the great moments' stings; zoomed in, the colours thin to a wash and then to their borders and banners, so that the ground, the season and the figures show through, and the sound comes from what is near the view (the waves around a ship, a column's march, a battle's clash), louder the nearer, with only a few sounds at once so that it stays clear and light on a phone; the map's views keep their colours at every zoom, since colour is what they show. Smooth on a phone, measured as item 19 measures it, in the busiest season, and held to 17a's bar: no frame over about 50 ms while a season plays, at every speed, on desktop and on a throttled phone, with the frame times and a short recording in the PR. And spectator mode points the viewer to what is worth watching (Haakon, 31 October 2026, to the design session's question on a list of threads to watch and an optional director camera: "And yes to" it): a list of threads to watch, the narrator's pick from the record of the few live stories with the most at stake this season (a bribed envoy on his road, a claimant's following rising, a siege a season from falling), each a click away (follow the person, open the message trail, take the map there), ranked by the stake the engine already measures for its model calls; and an optional director camera, off by default, that takes the map to the highest-stakes scene as the season plays out; both choose only what is shown, never what happens, never show a seat more than it knows, and work the same in replay from the record afterwards. And a mind's own words are kept and shown (Haakon, 31 October 2026, to the design session's question on showing them: "Yes, I think so. And it should maybe store what it looked like at every step? And the narrator should also have its take stored from the first time it runs on a game, so it must not be ran each time you watch it potentially afterwards?"): the record keeps, season by season, each model mind's notes, journal and plan as they stood then, storing only what changed so a game stays small, and the spectator's seat view shows them as written beside the seat's decisions and spoken words, as does every view once the game ends, never another seat during play; and everything the narrator writes (personas, the chronicle, the threads to watch, the legends) is stored in the record the first time it is written, so watching a game again reads it back and never calls a model again, unless the game's owner asks for it to be told anew, which keeps the first telling beside the new (Haakon, 31 October 2026: "Yes to both. But I think it should only show their name like that when you click on the character? Or di you want it in parenthesis in every letter they receive?"). Presentation only, built on 17a's stream of events; it may run beside item 18, and item 19++ then makes it beautiful. Then **17+++a, keys for everything** (Haakon, 31 October 2026: "pressing spacebar really needs to pause and unpause the game. Everything should have hotkeys for the computer quiet frankly, and Paradox hotkeys is what people are used to, so we should probably use those.", then "Agreed to all, expertly!"): on a computer every action has a key, after Paradox's own, since that is what players of the genre already know. Crusader Kings III is the base, as the closest of their games to this one, and Europa Universalis IV where it has no like, each key taken from the games' own key lists, not from memory: Space pauses and unpauses, even while a season plays out; 1 to 4 choose the pace ("Pace of play" under Interface): 1 Slow, 2 Normal, 3 Fast, 4 Simulate, and + and −, on the main keys and the number pad, step between Slow, Normal and Fast, matching the character typed, not the key's place, so + speeds up on every keyboard; Enter ends the season's orders when it is the player's turn, as in Civilization, since seasons are turns and time never runs between them (Haakon, 1 November 2026: "Yes, please! expertly! does the hotkeys become 1, 2, 3, and 4 then?"); Escape closes the window in front, and opens the menu when none is open; letters switch the map's views, as their map modes do, leaving W, A, S and D with the arrows to move the map; F-keys open the main windows (the seat, the realm, the armies, the letters, the council, the chronicle), as Crusader Kings III's F1 to F8 open its own; the wheel zooms. Each key shows in its button's tooltip, one page lists them all, each can be changed and is remembered between visits, and no key acts while a letter or a name is being typed. The phone is unchanged. Space and the speed keys come first, in the polish lane, so the live game has them at once. From then on each item that adds a window, a view or an action brings its key in the same item. Then **17++++, a small state as a seat** (31 October 2026; Haakon: "maybe there should be an option to play as one of the small states, even if that's not what represented at the front and adviced", then "Yes, expertly to all!"): any city-state's or chief's seat can be taken by a human or a model, as any Great King's can, from the same seat choice, marked as harder and not the advised start; it plays by the same rules with its own seat view, letters and council ("For every ruler played by a model or a human"), and is judged on the one scoreboard against its own start, as every power already is ("One scoreboard for every power", "Relative score"), so a Byblos that holds out and grows can win. Nothing checks which power a seat is; what the item adds is the seat choice and the seat view's fit for a small realm. Rib-Hadda of Byblos is the archive's own protagonist, begging Pharaoh for archers in letter after letter.
